source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT, session 4 group definitions
finding: Session 4 swapped tools. 'Reassigned LLM group' means people who had been Brain-only in sessions 1-3 and now used the LLM. 'Reassigned Brain-only group' means former LLM users now writing unaided. The 1/9 correct-quote group is the reassigned LLM group (Brain-to-LLM). The 7/9 group is the reassigned Brain-only group (LLM-to-Brain).
numbers: Session 4 N=18 (9 per reassigned group). Q5: 7/9 reassigned-LLM failed to quote vs 1/9 reassigned-Brain-only. Q6: 1/9 reassigned-LLM quoted correctly vs 7/9 reassigned-Brain-only, reported as significantly worse.
quote: Only one participant in reassigned LLM group (1/9) produced an accurate quote, whereas 7/9 participants in reassigned Brain-only group did so.
limits: Preprint marked 'under review'. 9 per cell. The earlier evidence lines a24/c27 had the direction labels reversed. The poor quoting tracks the tool used in the current session, not prior exposure, so it is not clearly a lasting memory deficit.
agent_relevance: Quoting failure follows the CURRENT use of the LLM, which fits an encoding-while-offloading cost rather than lasting damage. Do not cite the labels from a24/c27.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) quoting figures by session
finding: The 15/18 vs 2/18 quoting-failure figure is given in the Q3 results of sessions 1-3. The Discussion ties 15/18 to Session 1 and says only 6/18 still failed by Session 3.
numbers: LLM group 83.3% (15/18) failed to give a correct quote; Search Engine and Brain-only 11.1% (2/18) each. LLM vs each other group p<.001; Search vs Brain-only p=1.0. Session 1: none of the LLM group quoted correctly. Session 3: 6 of 18 still failed.
limits: Same preprint, N=18 per group, not peer reviewed. Deficit shrinks across sessions as people reuse the same topic.
agent_relevance: The effect is large at first contact and fades with repetition. Do not treat 83% as a steady-state figure.

source: Hesselmann (2020) Google Stroop replication, PeerJ; account of Camerer et al. (2018) Sparrow replication
finding: Camerer et al. 2018 (replication led by Holzmeister and Camerer) replicated Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Experiment 1, the Google Stroop priming test. It found no significant effect despite adequate power. The other Sparrow experiments (memory for statements, where-vs-what) are not mentioned as part of that project. Sparrow (2018) objected to design differences (words repeated, block-wise digit load, outdated 2006 computer terms). Hesselmann fixed those points and still found a null.
numbers: Original N=46 (2006). Camerer replication two-stage: stage 1 N=104, stage 2 N=234, pooled. Hesselmann N=117 tested, 89 in final analysis (as in K04), German sample, preregistered, 16 Internet words, no word repetition.
limits: Camerer replication used 8 Internet words and repeated words; original authors gave no materials. Priming, not memory, was tested. Gap 10: only Experiment 1 is confirmed as replicated by Camerer.
agent_relevance: The priming mechanism is out. The 'remember where' memory results stay unreplicated in the large replication projects, not refuted.

source: Gong and Yang (2024) Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review, Frontiers in Public Health
finding: Opened the full text. The review pools heterogeneous 'frequent Internet search' studies, sorted into cognitive load, cognitive measurement, behavioural phenotype, cognitive self-esteem and psychophysiology. It reports a 'moderate but significant' pooled effect, but the pooled d itself is not given in the text. Only region moderated heterogeneity.
numbers: 22 articles, 30,889 participants, ages 12 to 89, 908 records screened. Cognitive load subgroup 0.73 [0.22, 1.24]. Another subgroup 1.01 [-0.12, 2.13]. Region Q=6.20, p<.05, 13.18% of heterogeneity; North America -1.04 [-1.88, -0.20]. Publication bias judged by visual funnel plot only.
limits: Mixes self-esteem, survey and lab measures, so it is not a clean test of 'remember where not what'. Mobile phone and prior-knowledge claims are in the discussion, not a reported moderator test. The d range of -0.85 to 4.38 quoted earlier could not be found in the text.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for any single 'where not what' memory shift. Treat K03 as contested.

source: Wu, Wu and Zou (2024) ClashEval, NeurIPS D&B
finding: First direct measure of Twin Otto behaviour. With a wrong retrieved note, models often drop a correct own answer (context bias). With a right note, they rarely keep a wrong own answer (prior bias). The less confident the model was (token probability), the more it took the note. Rescaling the probabilities cut errors.
numbers: 1,200+ questions, 6 domains, 6 models. Table 4 context bias / prior bias / accuracy: Claude Opus 0.157 / 0.021 / 0.743; Claude Sonnet 0.201 / 0.025 / 0.658; Gemini 1.5 0.245 / 0.037 / 0.624; GPT-4o 0.304 / 0.021 / 0.615; GPT-3.5 0.313 / 0.028 / 0.539; Llama-3 0.264 / 0.021 / 0.500. Slope of note-preference vs prior confidence -0.1 to -0.45 per domain. Calibrated token-probability correction raised accuracy 14% overall and cut context bias 20% (GPT-4o 0.615 to 0.754 per Table 3 row order).
quote: LLMs are susceptible to adopting incorrect retrieved content, overriding their own correct prior knowledge over 60% of the time.
limits: The abstract says models override correct priors 'over 60%' of the time; the per-model tables show 15.7% to 31.3% over the whole set, so the 60% applies to a narrower condition I could not locate. Facts, not agent notes. Needs token probabilities. Mid-2024 models. Table 3 row labels were garbled in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 largely answered for facts: a wrong note is followed 16-31% of the time when the model was right; a correct note is ignored 2-4% of the time. Gap 3: the model's own confidence is a usable gate.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth, ICLR
finding: Models follow external evidence if it is coherent and convincing, even against their own memory. Yet when the evidence contains both a supporting and a conflicting piece, they cling to their own belief (confirmation bias). The bias is stronger for popular facts.
numbers: GPT-4 memorization ratio 80% on the most popular questions in the multi-source condition. 50 stubborn cases were hand-checked.
limits: Fact QA with generated counter-evidence, 2023 models. The mixed support-and-conflict condition is the realistic one for a notes store.
agent_relevance: A notes store with several mutually inconsistent entries will be resolved toward what the model already believes. Coherence of a note matters as much as its presence.

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When Not to Trust Language Models, ACL
finding: Retrieval helps for rare facts and can hurt for popular ones. A gate that retrieves only below a popularity threshold beat both never-retrieve and always-retrieve and cut cost.
numbers: PopQA 14k questions. For 10% of questions retrieval is harmful (retrieved text recall@1 0.14). Best result: GPT-3 davinci-003 with adaptive retrieval 46.5% accuracy, 5.3% above any non-adaptive method; API cost cut by roughly half.
limits: The gate uses entity popularity, a proxy for confidence, not the model's own confidence. One 2022 model family.
agent_relevance: Supports a consult-or-recall gate for gap 3. Gain over the best fixed policy was about 5 points at lower cost.

finding: A small classifier that picks no retrieval, one-step or multi-step per question sits between the cheap and the costly fixed policies on accuracy and time. The classifier is imperfect.
numbers: Classifier confusion: no-retrieval questions sent to one-step about 47% and to multi-step about 22% of the time; multi-step sent to one-step about 31%. Per-dataset tables were garbled in the PDF text and are not quoted.
limits: Read abstract, method and classifier analysis; per-dataset numbers not extracted. The gate is a trained classifier, not self-confidence.
agent_relevance: A gate is worth building but its own errors are large; keep it cheap and fail toward consulting.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: A compact self-curated memory beat no memory and beat appending the full history. It also beat a majority vote of 3 samples at roughly comparable token use. It is the closest equal-compute test found for gap 1.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024: baseline 23.3%, majority vote (3 samples) 23.3%, full-history append 26.7%, DC-Cu 50.0%. AIME 2025: 6.7% baseline and MV, 36.7% DC-Cu. GPT-4o AIME 2024: 20.0% baseline, 6.7% full history, 40.0% DC-RS. Mean tokens AIME 2024 for Sonnet: 370 baseline, 1,035 DC-RS, 1,831 DC-Cu. GPQA-Diamond Sonnet 59.6% to 68.7% DC-RS; GPT-4o only 57.1% to 58.1%; GPT-4o-mini some variants below baseline.
limits: Question streams within one benchmark, not separate user sessions. Tokens not matched exactly (3 samples is about 1,100 tokens vs DC-Cu 1,831). 30 questions per AIME set. Gains depend on model size and on similar questions recurring. Retrieval noise hurt GPT-4o on GPQA.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 1 for math: curated notes beat extra samples. Do not append raw history. Run our own test at exactly equal tokens.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Distilled strategies from both successes and failures beat raw trajectories (Synapse) and success-only workflows (AWM). Extra test-time compute helped much more with good memory than without it.
numbers: WebArena overall (684 tasks), Gemini-2.5-flash, k=5: No Memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, plus MaTTS 51.8. Scaling k from 1 to 5: with memory parallel 49.7 to 55.1, sequential 49.7 to 54.5; without memory it fluctuated 39.0 to 42.2 (parallel) and 37.4 to 40.6 (sequential). Vanilla TTS at k=5 52.4 vs MaTTS 55.1. Scaling lifted weaker memories little (Synapse 40.6 to 41.2, AWM 44.4 to 45.5).
limits: Google-authored, web and software tasks, self-judged success labels. Memory and compute are combined here, not traded off at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Memory and compute look like complements, not substitutes: compute paid off only with strong notes. Distilled notes beat raw trajectories in an agent setting (gap 7).

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: benchmarking test-time learning with self-evolving memory
finding: Across 10 streams and over ten memory modules, a plain experience-retrieval baseline (ExpRAG) outperformed several complex designs. The gain from the best method (ReMem) tracks how similar the tasks in a stream are.
numbers: Correlation of ReMem gain over the history baseline with within-dataset task similarity: Pearson 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). ReMem BabyAI 0.92/0.96 and ScienceWorld 0.95/0.62 in multi-turn tests. Hard-to-easy task sequence up to 0.94/0.97 success/progress.
limits: Google DeepMind and UIUC authors propose ReMem, so not neutral. I read the text; some table cells were unreadable in the PDF.
agent_relevance: Simple stores are hard to beat. Notes help when tasks recur; expect little gain on novel tasks.

source: Hu, Wang and McAuley (2026) MemoryAgentBench, ICLR
finding: An independent benchmark ranks memory systems very differently from vendor LoCoMo claims. Simple retrieval and long context beat the popular memory products. This addresses gap 4.
numbers: Overall score (GPT-4o-mini backbone; bare model 42.3): BM25 41.5, HippoRAG-v2 41.6, Text-Embed-3-Large 38.0, MemGPT 28.3, MIRIX 26.2, Zep 24.0, Mem0 21.1, Cognee 20.6, Self-RAG 18.7. Long-context GPT-4o 48.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 49.6; GPT-5-mini 60.6. Selective forgetting multi-hop: all methods at most 28%. Long-context models best on test-time learning and long-range understanding; RAG best on accurate retrieval.
limits: Mem0 and others ran with a uniform 4096-token chunk, which may disadvantage them. Different tasks from LoCoMo.
agent_relevance: Do not trust vendor LoCoMo rankings. Start with plain chunked retrieval. Test whether an updated note overrides an old one (selective forgetting).

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval, ICLR: note-format ablations
finding: Format ablation in a budget-aware setting. Splitting sessions into rounds helped GPT-4o. Replacing text with summaries or extracted facts hurt through information loss, except on multi-session reasoning. Indexing by raw text plus extracted facts (key expansion) was best. Structured JSON plus chain-of-note reading added up to 10 points even with perfect retrieval.
numbers: Key expansion with user facts: +9.4% recall@k and +5.4% final accuracy on average across models. Time-aware query expansion: +11.3% recall (rounds) and +6.8% (sessions). Suboptimal reading strategy: up to 10-point drop under oracle retrieval for GPT-4o.
limits: Chat-history memory, not agent skills. Facts alone as keys did not help.
agent_relevance: Store raw text and add facts as extra keys; do not replace text with summaries. The read-back prompt format matters as much as the store.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners, AAAI
finding: Abstracted insights beat raw successful trajectories on reasoning QA, raw trajectories beat insights on embodied action tasks, and WebShop is a tie. Gives gap 7 a domain split.
numbers: Insights-only / retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36% / 31%, ALFWorld 50% / 55%, WebShop 37% / 38%. ExpeL without retries matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%) and beats it on ALFWorld (59% vs 54%).
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 era; single runs; differences of about 5 points are small.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly answered: write insights for reasoning questions, keep trajectories for action sequences.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR
finding: Reflection gains in earlier work depended on an outside signal about correctness. Without it, self-reflection did not help and often hurt. This is a boundary condition on Reflexion-style notes.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle labels: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 82.0; HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-4 HotpotQA 29.0 to 59.0). Without oracle, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5.
limits: Tests same-episode self-correction, not written lessons reused in later episodes. Reflexion used test or environment feedback. Table text was partly garbled; numbers checked against two layouts.
agent_relevance: Write a reflection note only after an external check (test, tool result, user signal). Otherwise skip it.

finding: When the question shares no words with the stored fact, long contexts collapse. The lost-in-the-middle dip is visible in simple one-hop tests at 32K, but in two-hop tests accuracy falls everywhere, even at the edges.
numbers: GPT-4o 99.3 base to 69.7 at 32K. At 32K: Llama 3.3 70B 42.7, Gemini 1.5 Pro 48.2, Gemini 2.0 Flash 41.0, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 29.8, GPT-4o mini 13.7. 11 of 13 models below 50% of base at 32K. Effective length for GPT-4o 8K; most models 2K or less.
limits: Models tested up to early 2025 (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, Claude 3.5); no 2026 frontier model. Gap 6 stays open for current models.
agent_relevance: Keep the notes prompt short (a few K tokens) and put notes at the ends; placement cannot rescue a long mixed context.

source: Lurie, Fabrizio and Westerman (2025) The cost of saving: how photos and screenshots impair memory, Memory and Cognition
finding: Photo impairment replicated in three experiments, with screenshots and own phones. It did not grow with task complexity, which weakens the divided-attention account.
numbers: Memory worse for images saved by any method; screenshots worst despite being the simplest method. Earlier photo-impairment effect cited at d=1.25. Power analysis for N=36 per study.
limits: Undergraduates, art images. Saving costs the saved item, as K07 says.
agent_relevance: Supports K10: saving without processing costs memory of the saved item. For an agent, process before it files.

source: Cureus 2026 AI-assisted vs traditional learning and long-term retention in medical students
finding: In a within-subject comparison, AI-assisted study gave higher retention than traditional study at one week and one month. This points the other way from Kosmyna.
numbers: 149 enrolled, 115 base cohort, 95 with complete data. Retention at 1 week 75.5% vs 57.9%; at 1 month 61.4% vs 35.9% (p<.001). Learning method F=181.66; interaction F=62.23. Share above the high-retention benchmark 43.4% vs 3.0%.
limits: Different drug topics per condition (quinolones vs aminoglycosides), counterbalancing not seen, no randomisation, one site. The AI was a tutor, not a writing aid. Not a replication of Kosmyna.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no larger replication of the Kosmyna design found. The one outside result differs in task and design, so the AI memory cost depends on how the tool is used.
